questions.stem: What is the circumference of a circle of diameter 14 cm, using π ≈ 22/7?
questions.explanation: Circumference is πd, so 22/7 × 14 = 44 cm. Using the radius instead of the diameter halves the answer, which is the usual slip.

questions.stem: What is the area of a circle of radius 5 cm, to one decimal place?
questions.explanation: Area is πr² = π × 25 = 78.5 cm². The 31.4 answer is the circumference, which is what you get from 2πr instead.

questions.stem: A rectangle has area 60 cm² and length 12 cm. What is its width?
questions.explanation: Divide the area by the known length: 60 ÷ 12 = 5 cm. Subtracting instead of dividing is the error this question is set to catch.

questions.stem: A pencil is measured as 12.4 cm on a ruler marked in millimetres. What is the greatest possible error?
questions.explanation: The greatest possible error is half the smallest unit on the scale. The smallest division is 1 mm = 0.1 cm, so the error is 0.05 cm and the true length lies between 12.35 and 12.45 cm.

questions.stem: A garden bed is measured as 45 cm, correct to the nearest centimetre. What is the smallest it could be?
questions.explanation: Rounding to the nearest centimetre means the true value lies within half a centimetre, so the range is 44.5 to 45.5 cm and 44.5 is the lower limit.

questions.stem: A right-angled triangle has shorter sides 9 cm and 12 cm. Find the hypotenuse.
questions.explanation: By Pythagoras, c² = 81 + 144 = 225, so c = 15 cm. Answering 225 stops at the square of the length.

questions.stem: A cuboid measures 3 cm by 4 cm by 12 cm. Find its longest internal diagonal.
questions.explanation: Apply Pythagoras twice: the base diagonal is √(9 + 16) = 5, then the space diagonal is √(25 + 144) = 13 cm. A three-dimensional problem is nearly always two right-angled triangles in sequence.

questions.stem: What is the surface area of a closed cylinder with radius 3 cm and height 10 cm, to the nearest cm²?
questions.explanation: The net is two circles and a rectangle: 2πr² + 2πrh = 56.5 + 188.5 = 245 cm². Forgetting one or both circles is the standard omission.

questions.stem: What is the volume of a cylinder with radius 5 cm and height 10 cm, to the nearest cm³?
questions.explanation: Volume of a prism is the cross-section area times the length: πr²h = π × 25 × 10 = 785 cm³. Note the units are cubic.

questions.stem: A triangular prism has a cross-section of base 6 cm and height 4 cm, and a length of 10 cm. Find its volume.
questions.explanation: Cross-section area is ½ × 6 × 4 = 12 cm², then × 10 = 120 cm³. Forgetting the half is what gives 240.

questions.stem: Find the volume of a cone with radius 3 cm and height 8 cm, to one decimal place.
questions.explanation: A cone is a third of the cylinder that contains it: V = ⅓πr²h = ⅓ × π × 9 × 8 = 75.4 cm³. Leaving out the third gives 226.2, the volume of that whole cylinder.

questions.stem: Find the volume of a sphere of radius 6 cm, to one decimal place.
questions.explanation: V = (4/3)πr³ = (4/3) × π × 216 = 904.8 cm³. Cubing the radius rather than squaring it is the step to be careful with.

questions.stem: Find the surface area of a sphere of radius 5 cm, to the nearest cm².
questions.explanation: Surface area of a sphere is 4πr² = 4 × π × 25 = 314 cm². It happens to equal the curved surface of the cylinder that just contains it.

questions.stem: A square-based pyramid has base side 6 cm and perpendicular height 10 cm. Find its volume.
questions.explanation: A pyramid is a third of the prism with the same base and height: V = ⅓ × 36 × 10 = 120 cm³.

questions.stem: A cylinder of radius 4 cm and height 12 cm has a hemisphere of the same radius on top. What makes up the total outside surface?
options: Curved surface, one circle, and half a sphere
Curved surface and two full circles
Two full circles and a whole sphere
The curved surface of the cylinder only
questions.explanation: The base circle is still exposed, the top circle is covered by the hemisphere, and the hemisphere contributes half a sphere. Composite surface area is about which faces remain visible.

questions.stem: Convert 7.5 litres to millilitres.
questions.explanation: 1 litre is 1000 millilitres, so multiply by 1000. Remember also that 1 mL is exactly 1 cm³, which is the bridge between volume and capacity.

questions.stem: A tank has radius 40 cm and height 1 m. What is its capacity in litres, to the nearest litre?
questions.explanation: Work in centimetres: V = π × 1600 × 100 = 502655 cm³. Since 1000 cm³ is 1 litre, that is 503 litres. Mixing metres and centimetres is what makes this question hard.

questions.stem: How many square centimetres are there in 1 square metre?
questions.explanation: The conversion applies to both dimensions: 100 × 100 = 10 000 cm². For volume it applies three times, so 1 m³ is 1 000 000 cm³.

questions.stem: A shape is enlarged by a scale factor of 3. How do its area and volume change?
questions.explanation: Length scales by k, area by k² and volume by k³. With k = 3 that is 9 and 27 respectively.

questions.stem: A rectangle 10 cm by 6 cm has a 2 cm square cut from one corner. Find the remaining area.
questions.explanation: Find the whole rectangle and subtract the missing piece: 60 − 4 = 56 cm². Splitting it into two rectangles gives the same answer and takes longer.

questions.stem: What is the area of a circle with radius 5 cm, in exact form?
questions.explanation: Area is π times the radius squared, so 25π. Using the diameter or forgetting to square is what produces the other options.

questions.stem: What is the circumference of a circle with radius 7 cm, in exact form?
questions.explanation: Circumference is 2πr, so 14π. Squaring the radius gives the area instead, which is the most common confusion in this topic.

questions.stem: What is the volume of a cylinder with radius 3 and height 10, in exact form?
questions.explanation: Volume is the circular area times the height: π × 9 × 10 = 90π. A prism of any shape follows the same rule of base area times height.

questions.stem: What is the volume of a cone with radius 3 and height 10?
questions.explanation: A cone is exactly one third of the cylinder that contains it, so 90π ÷ 3 = 30π. The same one-third relationship holds for any pyramid and its prism.

questions.stem: What is the volume of a sphere with radius 3, in exact form?
questions.explanation: Volume is four thirds times π times the radius cubed: (4/3) × π × 27 = 36π. Cubing rather than squaring is what distinguishes volume from surface area.

questions.stem: How many cubic centimetres are in a litre?
questions.explanation: A litre is a cube 10 cm on each side, so 10 × 10 × 10 = 1000. This is why a millilitre and a cubic centimetre are the same volume.

questions.stem: Convert 2.5 square metres into square centimetres.
questions.explanation: A square metre is 100 × 100 = 10000 square centimetres, so multiply by that. Multiplying by 100 once is the error, because area conversions square the factor.

questions.stem: A cube has volume 64 cm³. What is its surface area?
questions.explanation: The side is the cube root of 64, which is 4. Each face is 16 cm² and there are six of them, so 96 cm². Finding the side first is the key step.

questions.stem: What is the area of a trapezium with parallel sides 6 and 10 and height 4?
questions.explanation: Average the parallel sides and multiply by the height: 8 × 4 = 32. The height must be the perpendicular distance, not a slanted side.

questions.stem: What is the area of a triangle with base 9 and perpendicular height 6?
questions.explanation: Half the base times the height gives 27. Forgetting to halve gives 54, which is the area of the rectangle that contains the triangle.

questions.stem: The surface area of a cylinder with radius r and height h is:
questions.explanation: There are two circular ends and one curved side that unrolls into a rectangle of width 2πr. The last option is the volume rather than an area.

questions.stem: What is the perimeter of a semicircle with radius 4, in exact form?
questions.explanation: Half the circumference is 4π, and the straight diameter of 8 closes the shape. Forgetting the diameter is the classic semicircle error.

questions.stem: A rectangle has area 48 cm² and width 6 cm. What is its perimeter?
questions.explanation: The length is 48 ÷ 6 = 8, so the perimeter is 2 × (6 + 8) = 28 cm. Finding the missing side first is what makes this two steps rather than one.

questions.stem: What is the length of the space diagonal of a 3 by 4 by 12 box?
questions.explanation: Apply Pythagoras twice: the base diagonal is 5, then √(25 + 144) = 13. The three-dimensional version squares all three edges and takes the root.

questions.stem: Convert 3.6 km/h into metres per second.
questions.explanation: Divide by 3.6, because there are 1000 metres in a kilometre and 3600 seconds in an hour. Multiplying instead gives a value far too large for a walking pace.

questions.stem: A circle has area 49π. What is its radius?
questions.explanation: Set πr² = 49π, so r² = 49 and r = 7. Working backwards from an area always involves a root, which is easy to forget.

questions.stem: What is the area of a sector that is a quarter of a circle with radius 8, in exact form?
questions.explanation: The full circle is 64π and a quarter of that is 16π. A sector area is always the fraction of the turn multiplied by the whole circle.

questions.stem: A sector has an angle of 60° in a circle of radius 6. What is its exact area?
questions.explanation: Sixty degrees is one sixth of a turn, and the full area is 36π, so the sector is 6π. Turning the angle into a fraction of 360° is the first step every time.

questions.stem: Which measurement needs a perpendicular height rather than a slant length?
questions.explanation: Area formulas use the perpendicular distance between the parallel sides. Using the slanted side always overestimates the area.

questions.stem: Two similar cones have heights 4 cm and 12 cm. How do their volumes compare?
options: The larger is 12 times the smaller
The larger is 27 times the smaller
The larger is 3 times the smaller
The larger is 9 times the smaller
questions.explanation: The length scale factor is 3, and volume scales by its cube, so 27. Length, area and volume scale by the factor, its square and its cube.

questions.stem: What is 1 hectare in square metres?
questions.explanation: A hectare is a square 100 m on each side, so 10000 square metres. It is the usual unit for land area in Australia.

questions.stem: A tank is a cylinder of radius 1 m and height 2 m. Roughly how many litres does it hold?
questions.explanation: The volume is π × 1 × 2, about 6.28 cubic metres, and each cubic metre is 1000 litres. Converting at the end keeps the arithmetic simple.
